items.title: Mary Carole McDonnell built a true-crime TV empire. Then the FBI came for her.
items.summary: Mary Carole McDonnell was added to the FBI's Most Wanted list in December 2025. Mark Harris for BI Mary Carole McDonnell needed cash. The veteran TV executive, whose company carved out a niche as a prolific producer of true-crime shows like "Corrupt Crimes" and "Motive to Murder," had racked up more than $1 million in debt in 2017 and was on the hunt for a cash infusion, court filings show. McDonnell was used to hustling: She told people she was heir to a famous aerospace fortune, but she started her television career from the bottom like everyone else, working her way up from secretary to chief executive over more than four decades in the business. Her employees whispered that the queen of true crime had done it while scarred by a terrible tragedy of her own: the murder of her 11-year-old sister in a botched kidnapping. When McDonnell approached a bank for a lifeline, she leaned on a dramatic backstory, claiming she was related to the founders of the McDonnell Douglas Corporation and was soon due $80 million from a family trust. Thanks to allegedly forged documents, she eventually obtained $14.6 million in loans. Not long after, McDonnell vanished, leaving behind her California life — her mansion, her Porsche, her adult sons — and a string of lawsuits from a bank and unpaid employees in her wake. The details of her past — the kidnapped sister, the bloodline, the inheritance — were revealed to be a fiction. She was, authorities said, a fraudster and a fugitive believed to have fled to Dubai. She was indicted on federal charges in 2018 and added to the FBI's Most Wanted list in 2025, becoming one of only 32 people to land on the list for white-collar crimes. How did a TV executive end up the star of a legal drama that could have been fodder for one of her own shows? Is McDonnell really in Dubai, and what happens to the cases against her in her absence? Business Insider reviewed hundreds of pages of court records and interviewed staff, producers, and ex-FBI agents who were on her payroll — along with someone who says they befriended her in Dubai — to reveal how McDonnell's story and her business unraveled. Mary Carole McDonnell is not actually an heiress or related to the family that built the McDonnell Douglas Corporation, the government and others have confirmed. A funeral notice for her father, Russell McDonnell, lists her as the fifth of six children born to Russell and Eva McDonnell, who owned McDonnell's Market Place, a beloved corner grocery that operated in Kirkwood, Missouri, for 75 years . The McDonnell Douglas Corporation merged with Boeing in 1997. Bettmann Archive After graduating from Principia College in 1974, McDonnell embarked on a career in television, bouncing around local stations and working her way up the ladder from secretary to producer to director of programming. By the 1990s, she'd moved to Los Angeles and become the vice president of programming and marketing at Argyle Television, now known as Hearst Television. In 1999, she became the vice president of programming at Raycom Media. While at Raycom, McDonnell launched her own production and distribution company, later called Bellum Entertainment, around 2005. It focused on shows on alien sightings like "Unsealed: Alien Files," the home remodeling show "Fix It & Finish It" starring soap star Antonio Sabato Jr., and shows stations needed to fill their Saturday morning educational and informational blocks like "Animal Atlas," "Zoo Clues," and "The Coolest Places on Earth." In 2014, McDonnell left Raycom to focus on Bellum full-time and needed funding. In 2015, she received a $2.7 million loan from Pacific Business Capital Corporation, according to a 2017 lawsuit Pacific later brought against her. When she applied for the loan, the lawsuit alleges, McDonnell claimed she had an $80 million trust, but couldn't provide details about the trust because of a tragic family story. A letter from McDonnell's attorney to the bank, viewed by Business Insider, said that McDonnell was unable to disclose any information or documentation related to the trust due to a court order issued after the "kidnap and murder" of her sister, Holly. In 2019, an arbitrator awarded Pacific Business Capital Corporation close to $6.8 million. McDonnell has not paid the judgment. There's no evidence that Holly was kidnapped. A 1966 St. Louis Post-Dispatch article says she was fatally stabbed in the back by a 14-year-old boy while playing in the yard of the McDonnell home. The two children knew each other from the schools for children with disabilities they attended. As McDonnell focused her full attention on Bellum, a lucrative trend in entertainment emerged: true crime . In the fall of 2014, the podcast "Serial" became a record-breaking phenomenon. Shortly after, the zeitgeist-defining success of two landmark docuseries, HBO's "The Jinx" and Netflix's "Making a Murderer," proved audiences had an insatiable appetite for the genre on television, too. An energized McDonnell was ready to position Bellum as a true-crime factory. Bellum began producing docuseries that could be made cheaply and syndicated widely. One of the first to take off was "Deep Undercover," which debuted in 2016 and was hosted by Joe Pistone, the FBI agent who famously went undercover in the mob using the name Donnie Brasco. Soon, Bellum was pumping out true-crime shows that aired everywhere from The CW to Investigation Discovery. "Motive to Murder," "Murderous Affairs," "Corrupt Crimes," "It Takes a Killer" — these weren't shows that were going to win Emmys, but they fed the industry's growing thirst for crime content. For Ethan LeCuyer, who started working at Bellum as an associate producer in 2015, life at Bellum at that time was good. It was a small, family-run operation, with McDonnell's nephew, Peter McDonnell, overseeing production on all the true-crime shows, and her twin sons, Sean and Mackenzie Carroll, working in post-production and sales and distribution, respectively. "There were only eight of us in total, including editors, so it was very tight-knit," LeCuyer told Business Insider in an exclusive interview about his time at Bellum. Everyone called Mary Carole 'MC,' even her sons, he said. He can't remember them ever calling her "mom." A still from "I Married a Murderer," one of Bellum's many true-crime shows. Bellum Entertainment LeCuyer was drawn to Bellum's scrappy, unconventional style: If he had to shoot B-roll for a show, he grabbed a camera and stole shots throughout Los Angeles, permits be damned. He often shot interviews at MC's mansion in La Cañada, an affluent suburb north of Los Angeles. "The house never seemed lived in, and it's filled with all this gaudy furniture. It almost felt like a set, but with the exception of maybe four or five pictures of Sean and Mack as kids," LeCuyer said. One aspect of the job concerned him: He said he rarely got paid on time, and when he did, the checks sometimes bounced. "The first time it happened, I was like, 'That's never happened to me before,' but you almost became numb to it a little bit because everybody was in the same boat," LeCuyer said. "It always cleared eventually." The Bellum playbook was simple: Shows were made by a scrappy few and done on the cheap. MC would go back out to buyers with new show ideas, get them sold, and use that money to fund the low-budget process all over again, LeCuyer and two other former Bellum executives told Business Insider. The strategy worked so well that by 2017, McDonnell had grander aspirations. That January, Cineflix, one of the UK's largest independent TV distributors, signed a distribution deal with Bellum. The same month, Bellum locked a multi-show deal with international distributor Red Arrow International, now known as Seven.One Studios, for over 200 hours of content. Between the new deals and existing ones with Sky Networks and Sinclair Broadcast Group, McDonnell was on a hot streak. Bellum would have to deliver a lot of fresh content — and fast. The company needed 26 episodes done in six months, said Andrew Nock, who was hired as the showrunner of season two of "Corrupt Crimes," a new Bellum show that would also be repurposed internationally under the name "Motive to Murder." The workload "seemed impossible," he said. So Nock hired extra people for several positions, reducing the favorable margins that Bellum had made the key to its success. Bellum also streamlined its operations with expert commentators, often retired FBI agents, who were hired to weigh in on the crimes discussed on shows. Instead of having them talk off the cuff about a case, producers crafted scripts they would memorize and repeat on-camera to save shooting and editing time. Interviews were moved from studios to the dingy basement of Bellum's office to save money. James R. Fitzgerald, a retired criminal profiler and forensic linguist whose work at the FBI led to the arrest of the Unabomber in 1996, was surprised to learn that he would be reading a script — and sometimes had to correct inaccuracies. Retired criminal profiler James R. Fitzgerald described being a commentator for Bellum as "a cookie-cutter enterprise." Donna Ward/Getty Images "It was going from Broadway to off-off-off-Broadway," Fitzgerald said, comparing Bellum to his previous commentating gigs. "It was a cookie-cutter enterprise." At one point, the company had 80 shows and 180 episodes in production, Nock said. Yet even when things were rocky, and paychecks came late, he said, "it seemed too big to fail." McDonnell made it seem that way, too. MC liked the finer things in life : She had a 4,805-square-foot, 5-bedroom La Cañada estate. She drove a Porsche. She owned a 39-foot boat docked in Newport beach. Every workday morning, she had a makeup artist do her glam in the office, two former Bellum employees told Business Insider. Her extravagances fomented frustration when paychecks were late. When they finally came, it was a struggle to get the money in hand. Nock and two other former Bellum employees said the checks would often bounce, and they would run to another bank that would sometimes cash them. "It was always a race to try to get there first to get your money," Nock said. "There was a woman at the… bank who would start laughing: 'Oh no, not more of these again!'" "We all knew we weren't going to see the money." Former Bellum story producer Bethany Jones Equipment and location vendors also clamored for their money. "We were doing this one story about a guy who killed his family on Christmas with a flamethrower, and I lent my Christmas tree for the shoot at this person's home in Burbank," Nock said. The homeowner "never got their check, and so they held my Christmas tree hostage." By the spring of 2017, it had become common for MC or her nephew, Peter, to make excuses as to why the staff wasn't getting paid on time, according to two former Bellum workers. In one instance, Deadline reported MC informed the company in a series of emails that Bellum had been a victim of bank fraud. In another, Peter told the staff there were issues with wire transfers, former Bellum story producer Bethany Jones said. Peter told Business Insider via email that he was unaware of any bank fraud. "I had no access to or information about the company's finances," said Peter, who left Bellum in July 2017 and says he's still owed over $10,000. "I began to suspect her explanations were lies," he said of his aunt. "The promise she made to everyone was that the company would soon receive a huge loan that would right the ship. It never came." As for the wire transfers, "I may have relayed an explanation from the CFO or Mary Carole about a payment delinquency," Peter wrote in his email. "Those delinquencies were becoming more common. If I added a reason for the delay, it was always based on the information I received. I stopped passing on explanations because I stopped trusting them myself." Some producers and crew members started taking drastic measures to get paid. Retired FBI special agent Bobby Chacon, who worked as a writer and technical advisor, said he saw a cameraman take an expensive camera home as collateral after a shoot, saying he hadn't been paid. Jones, who was a story producer on "I Married a Murderer" in 2016, said she stormed into the office one day with her IRS-credentialed tax preparer and confronted McDonnell, who turned pale and threatened to call the police on them. "It was an f-you," Jones told Business Insider in an exclusive interview as to why she confronted McDonnell. "We all knew we weren't going to see the money." Nock said one day, officials from the California Labor Commissioner's Office walked into Bellum unannounced. They "showed up one day with business cards and passed them out to everyone's desk because someone must have reported what was going on," he said. Aaron Cadieux took a different approach. After months of waiting for the $2,000 he says he was owed for working two-and-a-half days on an episode of Bellum's "Mysteries of the Unexplained," the filmmaker bought the domain name MaryCaroleMcDonnell.com and designed a disparaging webpage with a picture of McDonnell's head on a pig's body. An archived screenshot of Cadieux's webpage about McDonnell. Courtesy of Aaron Cadieux "I basically said, 'Look, I want my money. I own the domain name MaryCaroleMcDonnell.com. This is the website I've designed. If I don't get my money by Friday at 5 o'clock... this website is going to go live,'" Cadieux said, adding that he gave the company a week's notice of his intentions. "At like 4:55 p.m. on that Friday, they wired me my money." Cadieux still went live with the site in solidarity with the others who were never paid. Amid the workers' revolt, McDonnell gradually stopped showing up to the office, and the reality had sunk in that Bellum was on the verge of collapse. "That was the joke among us: You know the ship's sinking when Mary Carole will stop having her hair and makeup done every morning," Jones said. Around this time, the government alleges, McDonnell was trying to get money from banks. In March 2017, Reliable Fast Cash, which specialized in offering capital and merchant cash advances to small and midsize businesses, began to loan Bellum over $2.5 million, according to court documents. After months of partial payments, Bellum defaulted by July and again in August. Because McDonnell and her sons had signed documents agreeing to be liable for the debt in advance, a judge awarded Reliable over $3.3 million in September of that year, and the company immediately began collecting the debt. Over $550,000 in money and assets were seized from Sean and Mack, though they said they were unaware their signatures were on the loan application, according to court documents. The brothers filed a motion in 2019 to vacate the judgment, alleging that their mother forged their signatures on the loan. They settled with Reliable in 2020, with Reliable keeping the money it had already collected but agreeing not to withdraw any more. The family dynamic has been fraught ever since. People familiar with the family told Business Insider that Sean and Mack have not been in contact with their mother for years. Sean declined to comment; Mack did not respond. With her debts mounting, in December 2017, McDonnell applied for another loan, this time from Banc of California. Though McDonnell eventually secured over $14.6 million, it didn't solve Bellum's problems: By the end of the year, employees said, Bellum was effectively defunct. Records show Bellum officially became inactive in 2020. Close to 50 employees filed wage claims with the California Labor Commissioner's Office. In 2018, McDonnell was hit with both civil and criminal allegations. In July, Banc of California sued McDonnell in federal court, alleging that she falsely claimed to be an heir to the McDonnell Douglas Corporation aerospace fortune and was seeking millions to tide her over until she received a cash distribution from her family's $80 million trust. The bank said in court documents that it loaned McDonnell over $14.6 million after receiving loan documents it claims were false and forged. Banc of California later refiled the case in California state court, and a judge ruled in their favor in 2021 and awarded the bank over $17 million. On December 12, 2018, McDonnell was federally indicted on charges of bank fraud and aggravated identity theft. A page from McDonnell's 2018 indictment. United States District Court for the Central District of California With a warrant out for her arrest, McDonnell remained at large. McDonnell's exact movements are unknown, but the FBI has said it believes she had set down roots some 8,300 miles away from Hollywood, in Dubai. Dubai entrepreneur Thili Brady is used to rubbing shoulders with the wealthy and powerful. But when she met an older American woman nicknamed MC, something stood out: She introduced herself as an heiress and always brought it up. Brady struck up a friendship with McDonnell and her husband, Jeffrey Nilles, in 2019, after seeing them around the Dubai luxury hotel where she had an apartment. They shopped together, went to the movies, and had dinners. Brady described her bond with the couple as parental and said MC opened up to her new friend. "Each and every time she would get into my car, she would say, 'Oh, I had a Porsche back in the US,'" Brady said. MC said her kids would never call her, Brady added. "She'd get upset on special occasions and start crying. So I was feeling sorry for them." McDonnell and her husband, Jeffrey Nilles, in Dubai in a photo taken sometime after 2018. Courtesy of source MC approached Brady about getting into business, inviting her in 2019 to be part of a $7.5 million investment to develop three TV shows, according to an email Brady provided to Business Insider. "I have done these deals through banks before but this one requires private investment because of the immediate product demand," MC wrote. MC mapped out the path to generating revenue using the Bellum show "Motive to Murder" as an example, saying it generated $2 million in international sales in one year. "Crime series easily generate 4 to 5X return after recouping costs," she wrote. "The key to this is producing the shows in an 'evergreen' fashion so that the show easily has a 10 year amortization arc." MC estimated that in the US, she could sell each episode on cable for between $15,000 to $50,000, and sell an entire show to Netflix for $1 million a year. With revenue coming from cable, streaming, and syndication, MC predicted that it was "certainly doable" for investors to see a return on the $7.5 million within a year. Two former Bellum executives told Business Insider the figures in MC's email appear to have been inflated. Brady said she passed on the proposal after discussing it with a lawyer. "Her being an heiress was always brought up." Thili Brady, who met McDonnell in Dubai Brady remained friends with MC and Nilles until 2022, when she said the couple attempted to secure roughly $80,000 from her, then sued her for the money when she declined to pay them. Brady said she won the case and that Nilles appealed in 2024 and lost. Business Insider couldn't obtain detailed records of the case, but a public notice of appeal in Dubai shows Nilles appealed a case involving Brady in 2024. Nilles did not respond to a request for comment. After Brady fell out with McDonnell and Nilles, she did research and found a Facebook group for former Bellum employees. After she shared her experience with a member of the group, she said, the FBI interviewed her. Months later, Brady said, she bumped into McDonnell and Nilles in a parking lot. "They were like, 'You have insulted MC,'" Brady said. Brady said her parting comment to them was, "Karma is a bitch. This is going to come back to you." In December 2025, the FBI added McDonnell to its Most Wanted list. Suddenly, what had been a local story about unpaid employees in Hollywood was now national and international news: "Fake aerospace empire heiress, 74, lands on FBI's Most Wanted list for defrauding millions from banks," the New York Post headline blared. "A prolific true crime producer was truly a criminal the whole time, the FBI says," wrote The Guardian. A photo of McDonnell circulated by the FBI shows her blonde hair pulled back from her face, revealing pearl studs in her ears. She smiles broadly, appearing not to have a care in the world. McDonnell is one of only 32 people on the FBI's Most Wanted list for white-collar crimes. FBI FBI spokeswoman Laura Eimiller told Business Insider that the case is ongoing. "She's still a fugitive, and we believe she may be conducting fraud currently," she said. Eimiller also said the FBI believes McDonnell is in Dubai. If McDonnell is in Dubai, arresting her isn't as simple as sending American authorities to the UAE to serve a warrant. "Dubai is not a magic invisibility cloak, but it presents a significant legal and diplomatic obstacle," said Tom Simon, a former FBI special agent who now works as a private investigator with a specialty in fraud investigations. "The FBI cannot simply travel there, serve its warrant and put her on an airplane. Any arrest in Dubai requires the cooperation of Emirati authorities." However, arresting McDonnell wouldn't be impossible, Simon said. "Her location may provide protection from immediate arrest, but it does not provide permanent immunity." Back in the US, most ex-Bellum employees have since moved on with their lives. LeCuyer, who says he's owed over $10,000, worked as an EMT after Bellum and now works at a visual effects company. Fitzgerald, who still works as a commentator and co-hosts a true-crime podcast, says he's owed $10,000. Jones, who says she's owed $30,000, is working as a producer. Chacon, who says he's owed $36,000, is still a story consultant and expert commentator. One former Bellum contractor is still hoping he can get closure. Before McDonnell landed on the FBI's Most Wanted list late last year, Tim Clemente, a retired FBI counterterrorism agent who worked for Bellum as one of its crime experts, started hatching a plan to track down McDonnell. Retired FBI counterterrorism agent Tim Clemente worked as an expert commentator on Bellum's shows since 2014. Bellum Entertainment / Tubi Clemente, who says he's still owed around $5,000, described himself as a unique victim. "I got a lot of friends in the Middle East, I got a lot of friends in Dubai, Abu Dhabi, all over that area — special operations guys, foreign nationals that are over there working with United Arab Emirates special operations. I've done a lot of training." With the FBI now on the case, Clemente has stood down. Now, he can only wait for closure. Still, he dreams of giving the ordeal its own Hollywood ending. "I want to do it as an unscripted series," he said of the FBI's manhunt for McDonnell. "She used us for an unscripted series, and she made a lot of money. We would like to return the favor." items.summary_html:
Mary Carole McDonnell was added to the FBI's Most Wanted list in December 2025.

Mark Harris for BI

Mary Carole McDonnell needed cash.

The veteran TV executive, whose company carved out a niche as a prolific producer of true-crime shows like "Corrupt Crimes" and "Motive to Murder," had racked up more than $1 million in debt in 2017 and was on the hunt for a cash infusion, court filings show.

McDonnell was used to hustling: She told people she was heir to a famous aerospace fortune, but she started her television career from the bottom like everyone else, working her way up from secretary to chief executive over more than four decades in the business. Her employees whispered that the queen of true crime had done it while scarred by a terrible tragedy of her own: the murder of her 11-year-old sister in a botched kidnapping.

When McDonnell approached a bank for a lifeline, she leaned on a dramatic backstory, claiming she was related to the founders of the McDonnell Douglas Corporation and was soon due $80 million from a family trust. Thanks to allegedly forged documents, she eventually obtained $14.6 million in loans.

Not long after, McDonnell vanished, leaving behind her California life — her mansion, her Porsche, her adult sons — and a string of lawsuits from a bank and unpaid employees in her wake.

The details of her past — the kidnapped sister, the bloodline, the inheritance — were revealed to be a fiction. She was, authorities said, a fraudster and a fugitive believed to have fled to Dubai. She was indicted on federal charges in 2018 and added to the FBI's Most Wanted list in 2025, becoming one of only 32 people to land on the list for white-collar crimes.

How did a TV executive end up the star of a legal drama that could have been fodder for one of her own shows? Is McDonnell really in Dubai, and what happens to the cases against her in her absence? Business Insider reviewed hundreds of pages of court records and interviewed staff, producers, and ex-FBI agents who were on her payroll — along with someone who says they befriended her in Dubai — to reveal how McDonnell's story and her business unraveled.

Mary Carole McDonnell is not actually an heiress or related to the family that built the McDonnell Douglas Corporation, the government and others have confirmed. A funeral notice for her father, Russell McDonnell, lists her as the fifth of six children born to Russell and Eva McDonnell, who owned McDonnell's Market Place, a beloved corner grocery that operated in Kirkwood, Missouri, for 75 years.

The McDonnell Douglas Corporation merged with Boeing in 1997.

Bettmann Archive

After graduating from Principia College in 1974, McDonnell embarked on a career in television, bouncing around local stations and working her way up the ladder from secretary to producer to director of programming. By the 1990s, she'd moved to Los Angeles and become the vice president of programming and marketing at Argyle Television, now known as Hearst Television. In 1999, she became the vice president of programming at Raycom Media.

While at Raycom, McDonnell launched her own production and distribution company, later called Bellum Entertainment, around 2005. It focused on shows on alien sightings like "Unsealed: Alien Files," the home remodeling show "Fix It & Finish It" starring soap star Antonio Sabato Jr., and shows stations needed to fill their Saturday morning educational and informational blocks like "Animal Atlas," "Zoo Clues," and "The Coolest Places on Earth."

In 2014, McDonnell left Raycom to focus on Bellum full-time and needed funding. In 2015, she received a $2.7 million loan from Pacific Business Capital Corporation, according to a 2017 lawsuit Pacific later brought against her. When she applied for the loan, the lawsuit alleges, McDonnell claimed she had an $80 million trust, but couldn't provide details about the trust because of a tragic family story.

A letter from McDonnell's attorney to the bank, viewed by Business Insider, said that McDonnell was unable to disclose any information or documentation related to the trust due to a court order issued after the "kidnap and murder" of her sister, Holly. In 2019, an arbitrator awarded Pacific Business Capital Corporation close to $6.8 million. McDonnell has not paid the judgment.

There's no evidence that Holly was kidnapped. A 1966 St. Louis Post-Dispatch article says she was fatally stabbed in the back by a 14-year-old boy while playing in the yard of the McDonnell home. The two children knew each other from the schools for children with disabilities they attended.

As McDonnell focused her full attention on Bellum, a lucrative trend in entertainment emerged: true crime. In the fall of 2014, the podcast "Serial" became a record-breaking phenomenon. Shortly after, the zeitgeist-defining success of two landmark docuseries, HBO's "The Jinx" and Netflix's "Making a Murderer," proved audiences had an insatiable appetite for the genre on television, too.

An energized McDonnell was ready to position Bellum as a true-crime factory. Bellum began producing docuseries that could be made cheaply and syndicated widely. One of the first to take off was "Deep Undercover," which debuted in 2016 and was hosted by Joe Pistone, the FBI agent who famously went undercover in the mob using the name Donnie Brasco.

Soon, Bellum was pumping out true-crime shows that aired everywhere from The CW to Investigation Discovery. "Motive to Murder," "Murderous Affairs," "Corrupt Crimes," "It Takes a Killer" — these weren't shows that were going to win Emmys, but they fed the industry's growing thirst for crime content.

For Ethan LeCuyer, who started working at Bellum as an associate producer in 2015, life at Bellum at that time was good. It was a small, family-run operation, with McDonnell's nephew, Peter McDonnell, overseeing production on all the true-crime shows, and her twin sons, Sean and Mackenzie Carroll, working in post-production and sales and distribution, respectively.

"There were only eight of us in total, including editors, so it was very tight-knit," LeCuyer told Business Insider in an exclusive interview about his time at Bellum. Everyone called Mary Carole 'MC,' even her sons, he said. He can't remember them ever calling her "mom."

A still from "I Married a Murderer," one of Bellum's many true-crime shows.

Bellum Entertainment

LeCuyer was drawn to Bellum's scrappy, unconventional style: If he had to shoot B-roll for a show, he grabbed a camera and stole shots throughout Los Angeles, permits be damned. He often shot interviews at MC's mansion in La Cañada, an affluent suburb north of Los Angeles.

"The house never seemed lived in, and it's filled with all this gaudy furniture. It almost felt like a set, but with the exception of maybe four or five pictures of Sean and Mack as kids," LeCuyer said.

One aspect of the job concerned him: He said he rarely got paid on time, and when he did, the checks sometimes bounced.

"The first time it happened, I was like, 'That's never happened to me before,' but you almost became numb to it a little bit because everybody was in the same boat," LeCuyer said. "It always cleared eventually."

The Bellum playbook was simple: Shows were made by a scrappy few and done on the cheap. MC would go back out to buyers with new show ideas, get them sold, and use that money to fund the low-budget process all over again, LeCuyer and two other former Bellum executives told Business Insider. The strategy worked so well that by 2017, McDonnell had grander aspirations.

That January, Cineflix, one of the UK's largest independent TV distributors, signed a distribution deal with Bellum. The same month, Bellum locked a multi-show deal with international distributor Red Arrow International, now known as Seven.One Studios, for over 200 hours of content. Between the new deals and existing ones with Sky Networks and Sinclair Broadcast Group, McDonnell was on a hot streak. Bellum would have to deliver a lot of fresh content — and fast.

The company needed 26 episodes done in six months, said Andrew Nock, who was hired as the showrunner of season two of "Corrupt Crimes," a new Bellum show that would also be repurposed internationally under the name "Motive to Murder."

The workload "seemed impossible," he said.

So Nock hired extra people for several positions, reducing the favorable margins that Bellum had made the key to its success.

Bellum also streamlined its operations with expert commentators, often retired FBI agents, who were hired to weigh in on the crimes discussed on shows. Instead of having them talk off the cuff about a case, producers crafted scripts they would memorize and repeat on-camera to save shooting and editing time. Interviews were moved from studios to the dingy basement of Bellum's office to save money.

James R. Fitzgerald, a retired criminal profiler and forensic linguist whose work at the FBI led to the arrest of the Unabomber in 1996, was surprised to learn that he would be reading a script — and sometimes had to correct inaccuracies.

Retired criminal profiler James R. Fitzgerald described being a commentator for Bellum as "a cookie-cutter enterprise."

Donna Ward/Getty Images

"It was going from Broadway to off-off-off-Broadway," Fitzgerald said, comparing Bellum to his previous commentating gigs. "It was a cookie-cutter enterprise."

At one point, the company had 80 shows and 180 episodes in production, Nock said. Yet even when things were rocky, and paychecks came late, he said, "it seemed too big to fail."

McDonnell made it seem that way, too.

MC liked the finer things in life: She had a 4,805-square-foot, 5-bedroom La Cañada estate. She drove a Porsche. She owned a 39-foot boat docked in Newport beach. Every workday morning, she had a makeup artist do her glam in the office, two former Bellum employees told Business Insider.

Her extravagances fomented frustration when paychecks were late. When they finally came, it was a struggle to get the money in hand. Nock and two other former Bellum employees said the checks would often bounce, and they would run to another bank that would sometimes cash them.

"It was always a race to try to get there first to get your money," Nock said. "There was a woman at the… bank who would start laughing: 'Oh no, not more of these again!'"

"We all knew we weren't going to see the money."Former Bellum story producer Bethany Jones

Equipment and location vendors also clamored for their money.

"We were doing this one story about a guy who killed his family on Christmas with a flamethrower, and I lent my Christmas tree for the shoot at this person's home in Burbank," Nock said. The homeowner "never got their check, and so they held my Christmas tree hostage."

By the spring of 2017, it had become common for MC or her nephew, Peter, to make excuses as to why the staff wasn't getting paid on time, according to two former Bellum workers. In one instance, Deadline reported MC informed the company in a series of emails that Bellum had been a victim of bank fraud. In another, Peter told the staff there were issues with wire transfers, former Bellum story producer Bethany Jones said.

Peter told Business Insider via email that he was unaware of any bank fraud.

"I had no access to or information about the company's finances," said Peter, who left Bellum in July 2017 and says he's still owed over $10,000. "I began to suspect her explanations were lies," he said of his aunt. "The promise she made to everyone was that the company would soon receive a huge loan that would right the ship. It never came."

As for the wire transfers, "I may have relayed an explanation from the CFO or Mary Carole about a payment delinquency," Peter wrote in his email. "Those delinquencies were becoming more common. If I added a reason for the delay, it was always based on the information I received. I stopped passing on explanations because I stopped trusting them myself."

Some producers and crew members started taking drastic measures to get paid. Retired FBI special agent Bobby Chacon, who worked as a writer and technical advisor, said he saw a cameraman take an expensive camera home as collateral after a shoot, saying he hadn't been paid. Jones, who was a story producer on "I Married a Murderer" in 2016, said she stormed into the office one day with her IRS-credentialed tax preparer and confronted McDonnell, who turned pale and threatened to call the police on them.

"It was an f-you," Jones told Business Insider in an exclusive interview as to why she confronted McDonnell. "We all knew we weren't going to see the money."

Nock said one day, officials from the California Labor Commissioner's Office walked into Bellum unannounced.

They "showed up one day with business cards and passed them out to everyone's desk because someone must have reported what was going on," he said.

Aaron Cadieux took a different approach. After months of waiting for the $2,000 he says he was owed for working two-and-a-half days on an episode of Bellum's "Mysteries of the Unexplained," the filmmaker bought the domain name MaryCaroleMcDonnell.com and designed a disparaging webpage with a picture of McDonnell's head on a pig's body.

An archived screenshot of Cadieux's webpage about McDonnell.

Courtesy of Aaron Cadieux

"I basically said, 'Look, I want my money. I own the domain name MaryCaroleMcDonnell.com. This is the website I've designed. If I don't get my money by Friday at 5 o'clock... this website is going to go live,'" Cadieux said, adding that he gave the company a week's notice of his intentions. "At like 4:55 p.m. on that Friday, they wired me my money."

Cadieux still went live with the site in solidarity with the others who were never paid.

Amid the workers' revolt, McDonnell gradually stopped showing up to the office, and the reality had sunk in that Bellum was on the verge of collapse.

"That was the joke among us: You know the ship's sinking when Mary Carole will stop having her hair and makeup done every morning," Jones said.

Around this time, the government alleges, McDonnell was trying to get money from banks. In March 2017, Reliable Fast Cash, which specialized in offering capital and merchant cash advances to small and midsize businesses, began to loan Bellum over $2.5 million, according to court documents. After months of partial payments, Bellum defaulted by July and again in August.

Because McDonnell and her sons had signed documents agreeing to be liable for the debt in advance, a judge awarded Reliable over $3.3 million in September of that year, and the company immediately began collecting the debt. Over $550,000 in money and assets were seized from Sean and Mack, though they said they were unaware their signatures were on the loan application, according to court documents.

The brothers filed a motion in 2019 to vacate the judgment, alleging that their mother forged their signatures on the loan. They settled with Reliable in 2020, with Reliable keeping the money it had already collected but agreeing not to withdraw any more.

The family dynamic has been fraught ever since. People familiar with the family told Business Insider that Sean and Mack have not been in contact with their mother for years.

Sean declined to comment; Mack did not respond.

With her debts mounting, in December 2017, McDonnell applied for another loan, this time from Banc of California. Though McDonnell eventually secured over $14.6 million, it didn't solve Bellum's problems: By the end of the year, employees said, Bellum was effectively defunct. Records show Bellum officially became inactive in 2020. Close to 50 employees filed wage claims with the California Labor Commissioner's Office.

In 2018, McDonnell was hit with both civil and criminal allegations. In July, Banc of California sued McDonnell in federal court, alleging that she falsely claimed to be an heir to the McDonnell Douglas Corporation aerospace fortune and was seeking millions to tide her over until she received a cash distribution from her family's $80 million trust. The bank said in court documents that it loaned McDonnell over $14.6 million after receiving loan documents it claims were false and forged. Banc of California later refiled the case in California state court, and a judge ruled in their favor in 2021 and awarded the bank over $17 million.

On December 12, 2018, McDonnell was federally indicted on charges of bank fraud and aggravated identity theft.

A page from McDonnell's 2018 indictment.

United States District Court for the Central District of California

With a warrant out for her arrest, McDonnell remained at large. McDonnell's exact movements are unknown, but the FBI has said it believes she had set down roots some 8,300 miles away from Hollywood, in Dubai.

Dubai entrepreneur Thili Brady is used to rubbing shoulders with the wealthy and powerful. But when she met an older American woman nicknamed MC, something stood out: She introduced herself as an heiress and always brought it up.

Brady struck up a friendship with McDonnell and her husband, Jeffrey Nilles, in 2019, after seeing them around the Dubai luxury hotel where she had an apartment. They shopped together, went to the movies, and had dinners. Brady described her bond with the couple as parental and said MC opened up to her new friend.

"Each and every time she would get into my car, she would say, 'Oh, I had a Porsche back in the US,'" Brady said.

MC said her kids would never call her, Brady added. "She'd get upset on special occasions and start crying. So I was feeling sorry for them."

McDonnell and her husband, Jeffrey Nilles, in Dubai in a photo taken sometime after 2018.

Courtesy of source

MC approached Brady about getting into business, inviting her in 2019 to be part of a $7.5 million investment to develop three TV shows, according to an email Brady provided to Business Insider.

"I have done these deals through banks before but this one requires private investment because of the immediate product demand," MC wrote.

MC mapped out the path to generating revenue using the Bellum show "Motive to Murder" as an example, saying it generated $2 million in international sales in one year.

"Crime series easily generate 4 to 5X return after recouping costs," she wrote. "The key to this is producing the shows in an 'evergreen' fashion so that the show easily has a 10 year amortization arc."

MC estimated that in the US, she could sell each episode on cable for between $15,000 to $50,000, and sell an entire show to Netflix for $1 million a year. With revenue coming from cable, streaming, and syndication, MC predicted that it was "certainly doable" for investors to see a return on the $7.5 million within a year.

Two former Bellum executives told Business Insider the figures in MC's email appear to have been inflated.

Brady said she passed on the proposal after discussing it with a lawyer.

"Her being an heiress was always brought up."Thili Brady, who met McDonnell in Dubai

Brady remained friends with MC and Nilles until 2022, when she said the couple attempted to secure roughly $80,000 from her, then sued her for the money when she declined to pay them. Brady said she won the case and that Nilles appealed in 2024 and lost. Business Insider couldn't obtain detailed records of the case, but a public notice of appeal in Dubai shows Nilles appealed a case involving Brady in 2024. Nilles did not respond to a request for comment.

After Brady fell out with McDonnell and Nilles, she did research and found a Facebook group for former Bellum employees. After she shared her experience with a member of the group, she said, the FBI interviewed her.

Months later, Brady said, she bumped into McDonnell and Nilles in a parking lot.

"They were like, 'You have insulted MC,'" Brady said.

Brady said her parting comment to them was, "Karma is a bitch. This is going to come back to you."

In December 2025, the FBI added McDonnell to its Most Wanted list. Suddenly, what had been a local story about unpaid employees in Hollywood was now national and international news: "Fake aerospace empire heiress, 74, lands on FBI's Most Wanted list for defrauding millions from banks," the New York Post headline blared. "A prolific true crime producer was truly a criminal the whole time, the FBI says," wrote The Guardian.

A photo of McDonnell circulated by the FBI shows her blonde hair pulled back from her face, revealing pearl studs in her ears. She smiles broadly, appearing not to have a care in the world.

McDonnell is one of only 32 people on the FBI's Most Wanted list for white-collar crimes.

FBI

FBI spokeswoman Laura Eimiller told Business Insider that the case is ongoing. "She's still a fugitive, and we believe she may be conducting fraud currently," she said. Eimiller also said the FBI believes McDonnell is in Dubai.

If McDonnell is in Dubai, arresting her isn't as simple as sending American authorities to the UAE to serve a warrant.

"Dubai is not a magic invisibility cloak, but it presents a significant legal and diplomatic obstacle," said Tom Simon, a former FBI special agent who now works as a private investigator with a specialty in fraud investigations. "The FBI cannot simply travel there, serve its warrant and put her on an airplane. Any arrest in Dubai requires the cooperation of Emirati authorities."

However, arresting McDonnell wouldn't be impossible, Simon said. "Her location may provide protection from immediate arrest, but it does not provide permanent immunity."

Back in the US, most ex-Bellum employees have since moved on with their lives. LeCuyer, who says he's owed over $10,000, worked as an EMT after Bellum and now works at a visual effects company. Fitzgerald, who still works as a commentator and co-hosts a true-crime podcast, says he's owed $10,000. Jones, who says she's owed $30,000, is working as a producer. Chacon, who says he's owed $36,000, is still a story consultant and expert commentator.

One former Bellum contractor is still hoping he can get closure.

Before McDonnell landed on the FBI's Most Wanted list late last year, Tim Clemente, a retired FBI counterterrorism agent who worked for Bellum as one of its crime experts, started hatching a plan to track down McDonnell.

Retired FBI counterterrorism agent Tim Clemente worked as an expert commentator on Bellum's shows since 2014.

Bellum Entertainment / Tubi

Clemente, who says he's still owed around $5,000, described himself as a unique victim. "I got a lot of friends in the Middle East, I got a lot of friends in Dubai, Abu Dhabi, all over that area — special operations guys, foreign nationals that are over there working with United Arab Emirates special operations. I've done a lot of training."

With the FBI now on the case, Clemente has stood down. Now, he can only wait for closure. Still, he dreams of giving the ordeal its own Hollywood ending.

"I want to do it as an unscripted series," he said of the FBI's manhunt for McDonnell. "She used us for an unscripted series, and she made a lot of money. We would like to return the favor."

items.title: A couple bought an RV to live in full time. They're hoping to explore every state in their retirement on the road.
items.summary: Kristen and Dan Koepke recently started RV living. Kristen and Dan Koepke Kristen and Dan Koepke are exploring a new chapter: retirement and RV living. They bought an RV for $85,000, made some upgrades, and expect to spend on excursions as they travel. They think this change works if you're fine with downsizing and living without a stationary base. Kristen, 44, and Dan Koepke, 57, recently started a new chapter of their lives: learning what it's like to live full-time in an RV as retirees . Several years ago, Kristen had a bucket list goal of visiting the state capital, a park or forest, a landmark, and "any other key hot spots" in every state by RV, so the Koepkes could actually experience what each state has to offer. Dan was hesitant at first, but quickly got on board after hearing stories from visitors to the couple's Wisconsin winery who enjoyed the RV life. They put the dream aside and continued running their business, which they had been operating since 2013. When they were approached by a potential buyer for their winery in 2023, it was the perfect time to revisit their RV life idea and early retirement. It's been over a month of RV living, and the Koepkes are loving sightseeing, hiking, and visiting historical places, with no plan to stop traveling. While traveling, the Koepkes will be participating in various activities, such as horseback riding. Kristen and Dan Koepke The Koepkes and their dog, Vinny, are among the many Americans who have pivoted to living and traveling in an RV. Patty and Shane Gill have traveled in an RV in all 50 states, and Anne and Brian Klumpp hope to reach that same milestone. RVers range from families with young children to empty-nest retirees. Have you downsized from a house to an RV or from a large space to a tiny home? Reach out to this reporter to share at mhoff@businessinsider.com. Learning what RV life is like Kristen was in charge of accounting and staff management at the winery before it closed last September. She also worked part-time at a gym. Dan, who was the winery's main winemaker, also worked in tech for decades. Dan said he was saving a lot because he always wanted to retire around his mid-50s. He resigned from his senior director of information security job toward the end of May, at a company he had been with for five years. He was eager to get on the road after the couple bought the RV in August. They had to wait because there were some logistical issues with the sale of their winery, which was a separate sale from the original one in 2023. While the final sale is still pending, they hit the road as planned. The Koepkes said that "if you can mentally get past selling virtually all your possessions, learn how to move around and communicate efficiently in small spaces," and be fine without a stationary home base, it's a lifestyle change that can work. Kristen and Dan Koepke are exploring the country with their dog, Vinny. Kristen and Dan Koepke They're adjusting and learning as they go, such as remembering to pack enough water and snacks for themselves and their dog, and to download maps before heading into the wilderness. Dan wished they had a coffee pot for high altitudes, while Kristen wished they had started preparing for the transition earlier. There was a lot to do, "from selling things to moving our few saved items to storage and even packing the RV," she said, and it felt like they were rushing at the end. With higher prices , the Koepkes expect to spend more on gas a month in their Jeep, which they tow behind the RV, than they originally thought they would, but their RV fuel costs are on par with what they expected. Kristen thinks people who want to travel should be careful of higher prices on groceries and dining in tourist areas. The couple will be spending more on excursions than before RV life, such as horseback riding, helicopter tours, and rafting. They hope to see all of the state capitals, checking off Pierre, South Dakota, so far. They also enjoyed visiting Devils Tower National Monument in Wyoming. They found Yellowstone stunning but a somewhat challenging visit since dogs aren't allowed on trails. Kristen and Dan Koepke at Yellowstone. Kristen and Dan Koepke Buying their new home The Koepkes bought a 29-foot RV Class C toy hauler for $85,000. That type of vehicle includes a garage space, where they can store their motorcycles. They got rid of a lot of their belongings, making several runs to donate items to Goodwill and selling other items. Dan said he's a minimalist, so getting rid of a lot of their stuff was relieving. The couple said Class C toy haulers are rare in the US. They got in touch with an autotrader in Rhode Island and flew to pick it up. "Never met the guy before, just went to his house and with a check in hand to pick this up and drive it home," Kristen said. Kristen and Dan Koepke's RV and Jeep. Kristen and Dan Koepke Dan said driving the RV was easier than expected, and they got to experience what it would be like to maneuver it with wind, rain, construction, and traffic on their trip back to Wisconsin. They made some upgrades so they can go off-grid when they want, totaling over $2,900. That included adding another solar panel to the roof, which required other upgrades so they can run more items, and installing Starlink Mini for internet. Dan said the upgrades mean they can comfortably camp at places without electricity or other hookups because they can run their coffee pot and LED lights, watch television, and use the computer without issues. They also switched the mattress to something more comfortable than what's typically in RVs, which they said was a game changer. They're also keeping up an active lifestyle on the road, bringing exercise bands, a medicine ball, and a yoga mat. Kristen mapped out the first few months of their trip in advance, but the couple doesn't want to rush through states. Kristen said they want to sightsee and explore the area to count it as visiting. They plan to visit the southern states in the winter and eventually go through Canada to visit Kristen's brother in Alaska. They will miss their friends, but will see some of them who enjoy camping. They're also excited for their dog, who enjoys walks and socializing after growing up on the winery patio. Are you pursuing RV life? Reach out to this reporter to share at mhoff@businessinsider.com . Kristen, 44, and Dan Koepke, 57, recently started a new chapter of their lives: learning what it's like to live full-time in an RV as retirees.

Several years ago, Kristen had a bucket list goal of visiting the state capital, a park or forest, a landmark, and "any other key hot spots" in every state by RV, so the Koepkes could actually experience what each state has to offer. Dan was hesitant at first, but quickly got on board after hearing stories from visitors to the couple's Wisconsin winery who enjoyed the RV life.

They put the dream aside and continued running their business, which they had been operating since 2013. When they were approached by a potential buyer for their winery in 2023, it was the perfect time to revisit their RV life idea and early retirement.

It's been over a month of RV living, and the Koepkes are loving sightseeing, hiking, and visiting historical places, with no plan to stop traveling.

While traveling, the Koepkes will be participating in various activities, such as horseback riding.

Kristen and Dan Koepke

The Koepkes and their dog, Vinny, are among the many Americans who have pivoted to living and traveling in an RV. Patty and Shane Gill have traveled in an RV in all 50 states, and Anne and Brian Klumpp hope to reach that same milestone. RVers range from families with young children to empty-nest retirees.

Have you downsized from a house to an RV or from a large space to a tiny home? Reach out to this reporter to share at mhoff@businessinsider.com.

Learning what RV life is like

Kristen was in charge of accounting and staff management at the winery before it closed last September. She also worked part-time at a gym. Dan, who was the winery's main winemaker, also worked in tech for decades. Dan said he was saving a lot because he always wanted to retire around his mid-50s. He resigned from his senior director of information security job toward the end of May, at a company he had been with for five years. He was eager to get on the road after the couple bought the RV in August.

They had to wait because there were some logistical issues with the sale of their winery, which was a separate sale from the original one in 2023. While the final sale is still pending, they hit the road as planned.

The Koepkes said that "if you can mentally get past selling virtually all your possessions, learn how to move around and communicate efficiently in small spaces," and be fine without a stationary home base, it's a lifestyle change that can work.

Kristen and Dan Koepke are exploring the country with their dog, Vinny.

Kristen and Dan Koepke

They're adjusting and learning as they go, such as remembering to pack enough water and snacks for themselves and their dog, and to download maps before heading into the wilderness.

Dan wished they had a coffee pot for high altitudes, while Kristen wished they had started preparing for the transition earlier. There was a lot to do, "from selling things to moving our few saved items to storage and even packing the RV," she said, and it felt like they were rushing at the end.

With higher prices, the Koepkes expect to spend more on gas a month in their Jeep, which they tow behind the RV, than they originally thought they would, but their RV fuel costs are on par with what they expected. Kristen thinks people who want to travel should be careful of higher prices on groceries and dining in tourist areas.

The couple will be spending more on excursions than before RV life, such as horseback riding, helicopter tours, and rafting. They hope to see all of the state capitals, checking off Pierre, South Dakota, so far. They also enjoyed visiting Devils Tower National Monument in Wyoming. They found Yellowstone stunning but a somewhat challenging visit since dogs aren't allowed on trails.

Kristen and Dan Koepke at Yellowstone.

Kristen and Dan Koepke

Buying their new home

The Koepkes bought a 29-foot RV Class C toy hauler for $85,000. That type of vehicle includes a garage space, where they can store their motorcycles. They got rid of a lot of their belongings, making several runs to donate items to Goodwill and selling other items. Dan said he's a minimalist, so getting rid of a lot of their stuff was relieving.

The couple said Class C toy haulers are rare in the US. They got in touch with an autotrader in Rhode Island and flew to pick it up. "Never met the guy before, just went to his house and with a check in hand to pick this up and drive it home," Kristen said.

Kristen and Dan Koepke's RV and Jeep.

Kristen and Dan Koepke

Dan said driving the RV was easier than expected, and they got to experience what it would be like to maneuver it with wind, rain, construction, and traffic on their trip back to Wisconsin.

They made some upgrades so they can go off-grid when they want, totaling over $2,900. That included adding another solar panel to the roof, which required other upgrades so they can run more items, and installing Starlink Mini for internet. Dan said the upgrades mean they can comfortably camp at places without electricity or other hookups because they can run their coffee pot and LED lights, watch television, and use the computer without issues.

They also switched the mattress to something more comfortable than what's typically in RVs, which they said was a game changer. They're also keeping up an active lifestyle on the road, bringing exercise bands, a medicine ball, and a yoga mat.

Kristen mapped out the first few months of their trip in advance, but the couple doesn't want to rush through states. Kristen said they want to sightsee and explore the area to count it as visiting. They plan to visit the southern states in the winter and eventually go through Canada to visit Kristen's brother in Alaska.

They will miss their friends, but will see some of them who enjoy camping. They're also excited for their dog, who enjoys walks and socializing after growing up on the winery patio.

Are you pursuing RV life? Reach out to this reporter to share at mhoff@businessinsider.com.

items.title: AI is good, we swear! Trust us!
items.summary: iStock; Tyler Le/BI Meta's new ad is a Lisa Frank wet dream. There are rainbows, butterflies, bear hugs, and smash-cuts between three grinning children. It's a smiley, cloying vision for AI. The ad's narrator beckons us to call Meta's staff "optimists" and "dreamers," and says that the company is "betting on people" — tell that to the 8,000 workers Meta just laid off. It promises that the "future is for everyone" — a surprisingly collectivist mission for a company that has recently hired several acolytes of Donald Trump. While Meta turns up the cheer on AI, the American public has soured. 40% of Americans predict that AI will have a negative impact on society, according to Pew Research Center ; only 16% said it would be positive. Nearly three-quarters of Americans are opposed to data centers being built in their area, per Gallup. Protests abound, on TikTok, at City Halls, and outside Anthropic's headquarters . Meta clearly has something to prove — as do all the AI labs. As executives at Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and beyond change their tone from "AI could wipe out white-collar work" to "AI will be an immaculate boon for humanity," the industry's power players have gone on the defensive. AI is great, they say. We're leading it with joy and conscientiousness, they say. Trust us, they say. AI is a unique marketing challenge. A few years ago, it was described as all-powerful — the technological shift to end all technological shifts. It was "even bigger" than a technological revolution, Sam Altman said four months after ChatGPT's launch. Dario Amodei analogized LLMs to a "country of geniuses in a datacenter." Then there was the productivity wave, promising workers that it would make their jobs so much easier. If you believe Elon Musk, you might not need to work at all. And then there's always China, the looming threat the labs can cite to justify their breakneck speed. The China warnings aren't going away anytime soon. For all the giddiness of the Meta ad, Sean Spicer reacted with a dour warning. "The US can't lose the AI race to China," the former White House press secretary and onetime "Dancing With The Stars" contestant wrote in a quote tweet of the ad. I emailed Spicer to ask for his thoughts on the ad and what he thought it said about public opinion. He ignored the question. "There is no second place in the race to dominate AI," he wrote. That's what the AI race has long been about: domination. The labs have tried to dominate in pricing, in talent, in subtle digs on the podcast circuit. Can they soften their image to regain trust? Anthropic tried with its own barnburner of an ad that it debuted during the World Cup two weeks ago. It showed some terrifying images — facial recognition tracking, a cemetery, and yes, a burning house — while posing some terrifying questions. "Can AI be trusted?" a voiceover asked. "Who's gonna hit the brakes if we need to?" The answer: Anthropic! We here for you . If the ads prove anything, it's that the AI labs realize how deep the worries have gone. The ad was widely skewered. Andreessen Horowitz partner Olivia Moore wondered if Anthropic was "actively trying to churn users." Sam Altman wrote that he thought it was satire. And yet, its structure was remarkably similar to the Meta ad in one way: teeing up the criticism, then shutting it down. Anthropic gives its critics a pat on the head. "If we all had a voice in it, then I feel like it would be better," one voice in the ad says, implying that the public has a voice in Anthropic's development. They don't; it's not even a public company yet. The startup's message that there's "hope in hard questions" doesn't offer any plans for answering them. Meta, on the other hand, gives its critics the business. "Some people will have you believe AI will make us less connected," the ad's narrator says. "Have you believe" — what is this, hypnosis? Of course, Meta is the savior against these faceless snake-charmers. They're the optimists, the shining knights of the AI race. It's not just the LLM giants. Notion played into the criticism in its latest campaign: "AI dread" billboards . The software company set up a hotline for callers with a "nagging worry that AI can do our jobs." Trust is hard to earn. It's not clear that either strategy — the head-pat, the retort — will bring AI's detractors any peace. Some commenters loved the Meta ad, calling it a solve for growing doomerism. Others called called it "distasteful" and "unbelievably out of touch." Many mocked the score choice: David Bowie's "Five Years," a song about the demise of planet Earth. David Reibstein, a professor of marketing at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School, said that the AI labs had to address growing criticism. Anthropic's ad was "gutsy," he said, while he was less inspired by Meta's. The message is "trust us because we're Facebook," he said. On the criticism that Anthropic raised potential harms that the company itself was abetting those potential harms, he said, "I don't think it's being hypocritical. I think it's being sensitive." When reached for comment, a Meta representative sent contact information for some advertising executives it said the company had no financial ties to. One of these was Zach Blume , president of the creative agency Portal A, who said he found both ads "powerful and persuasive." I also asked Joonas Virtanen, a founding designer at the mini-app startup Wabi who had previously helped make Airbnb's chatbots "more fun," what he made of the campaigns. He said that he was more likely to believe Anthropic's approach, calling it an "honest" ad that "treats people like adults." As for Meta, he spat out the sugary sweetness. "It's a little bit of corporate bullshit," he said. "It is selling that rosy vision." Virtanen works in tech; he's predisposed to AI's benefits. The companies will need to bring in those outside the bubble, those who would rather live near a nuclear reactor than a data center. They'll be harder to convince. Sure, Amodei has tapered down his warnings of the oncoming AI apocalypse. And sure, Altman said he'd be "delighted to be wrong" about AI job destruction. But the seed is already planted. If the ads prove anything, it's that the AI labs realize how deep the worries have gone. They'll need more than rainbows and "hard questions" to uproot it. Henry Chandonnet is a reporter on the Business News desk. He mainly writes about AI and tech culture. Read the original article on Business Insider

Some commenters loved the Meta ad, calling it a solve for growing doomerism. Others called called it "distasteful" and "unbelievably out of touch." Many mocked the score choice: David Bowie's "Five Years," a song about the demise of planet Earth.

David Reibstein, a professor of marketing at the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School, said that the AI labs had to address growing criticism. Anthropic's ad was "gutsy," he said, while he was less inspired by Meta's. The message is "trust us because we're Facebook," he said. On the criticism that Anthropic raised potential harms that the company itself was abetting those potential harms, he said, "I don't think it's being hypocritical. I think it's being sensitive."

items.title: I’m a former McKinsey consultant who finally found joy after leaving the corporate world to start my own microbakery
items.summary: Hali Mo, a former consultant and product manager, quit her corporate job to start Hali Home Bakes after attending pastry school in Paris. Katherine Li/Business Insider Hali Mo quit her corporate job to start Hali Home Bakes after attending pastry school in Paris. Mo said she found her corporate job unfufilling and that she used to wake up to a sense of dread. Mo is still navigating the challenges of being a small-business owner, but her brand is growing. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Hali Mo , founder of Hali Home Bakes, a San Francisco microbakery specializing in laminated pastries. The essay has been edited for length and clarity. When I graduated from Stanford in 2018 with degrees in economics and computer science, I did what I thought I was supposed to do. I joined McKinsey as a business analyst, then moved into design consulting before becoming a product manager at a startup. On paper, everything looked right: good salary, clear career progression , prestigious companies. After five years in corporate America , I realized I was waking up every day dreading work. I turned 29 and thought, "I don't want to live like this." I quit my job, planning to take a year off — not to become a baker, but simply to figure out what actually made me happy. That decision eventually led me to pastry school in Paris, a microbakery that started in my apartment kitchen, and a completely different life than the one I'd imagined for myself. I followed the path I thought I was supposed to Growing up, I never had a crystal-clear dream job. Consulting appealed to me because it was practical. After two years at McKinsey, I moved into product management for a startup. I thought changing roles might solve the problem. It didn't. The work itself wasn't fulfilling for me. Every morning, I'd wake up dreading the day ahead while feeling guilty because I knew I was fortunate. I had stability, a good paycheck , and a career that made sense from the outside. Walking away from that felt almost irresponsible. Eventually, I realized I needed to stop asking what looked impressive and start asking what actually brought me joy. Pastry school in Paris changed everything Baking was my serious hobby for years. If someone had asked me for one bucket-list item, it would have been attending pastry school in France . So in early 2024, I quit my product management job and moved to Paris. I loved being a student again. After years of working, it felt like such a privilege to ask questions without worrying about performance reviews or promotions. I started posting videos about pastry school. Those videos unexpectedly took off on social media, and by the time I returned to the US, I had an audience that gave me the confidence to ask, "What if I tried selling pastries?" I moved to New York, where my partner lived at the time, bought a tiny convection oven and a countertop dough sheeter, and started baking under a cottage food license . My first preorder sold just 40 pastries. For the first few months, selling even a dozen boxes felt difficult. But gradually people came back, word of mouth spread, and social media continued to grow. By spring, I realized this could actually become something. By fall, I was consistently selling out pop-ups with lines of customers. It felt like every small success gave me permission to keep going. Starting over in San Francisco Mo is testing a July special pastry in her kitchen. Katherine Li/Business Insider Then my eight-year relationship ended. Suddenly, it felt like every part of my life was starting over. Personally, I was rebuilding after the breakup. Professionally, I was leaving behind the customer base I'd spent months building in New York. I moved back to San Francisco in January and essentially started from scratch. Fortunately, I knew much more than I had the first time around. Within months, I rebuilt my customer base and found a commercial kitchen that could support the specialized equipment I needed. Now I'm producing around 400 pastries each week and plan to expand to 1,000 with the help of a part-time baking assistant I'm looking to hire. The trade-offs are real — but so is the joy Running your own business comes with freedoms I never had in corporate life . I love setting my own schedule and building the kind of workplace culture I want. But there are trade-offs . There is no paid time off. If I get sick, there are no pastries to sell and no income. I pay for my own health insurance. I haven't had employer 401(k) contributions, and in my first two years as a business owner, I couldn't contribute to a traditional retirement account because I wasn't paying myself enough. Starting a small business also means funding your own runway. You're spending money long before you're making much of it. I think the biggest mindset shift has been believing in myself When I first started the bakery, I was half in and half out. Part of me assumed I'd probably end up going back to corporate. That hesitation made me pass on opportunities and avoid investments that would have helped the business grow. Now my mindset is completely different. I believe this business will succeed because I believe in my product and my ability to make it succeed. I don't think everyone should quit their corporate jobs. Some people genuinely love traditional careers, and that's wonderful. But if you've done the introspection, you have the financial runway, and you know deep down that your work is making you miserable, don't be afraid to take the next reasonable step . Life is too short to wake up every morning with a sense of dread. I feel incredibly lucky that now, when I wake up, I feel joy instead. Read the original article on Business Insider

Hali Mo, a former consultant and product manager, quit her corporate job to start Hali Home Bakes after attending pastry school in Paris.

Katherine Li/Business Insider

  • Hali Mo quit her corporate job to start Hali Home Bakes after attending pastry school in Paris.
  • Mo said she found her corporate job unfufilling and that she used to wake up to a sense of dread.
  • Mo is still navigating the challenges of being a small-business owner, but her brand is growing.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Hali Mo, founder of Hali Home Bakes, a San Francisco microbakery specializing in laminated pastries. The essay has been edited for length and clarity.

When I graduated from Stanford in 2018 with degrees in economics and computer science, I did what I thought I was supposed to do. I joined McKinsey as a business analyst, then moved into design consulting before becoming a product manager at a startup. On paper, everything looked right: good salary, clear career progression, prestigious companies.

After five years in corporate America, I realized I was waking up every day dreading work. I turned 29 and thought, "I don't want to live like this."

I quit my job, planning to take a year off — not to become a baker, but simply to figure out what actually made me happy.

That decision eventually led me to pastry school in Paris, a microbakery that started in my apartment kitchen, and a completely different life than the one I'd imagined for myself.

I followed the path I thought I was supposed to

Growing up, I never had a crystal-clear dream job. Consulting appealed to me because it was practical.

After two years at McKinsey, I moved into product management for a startup. I thought changing roles might solve the problem.

It didn't.

The work itself wasn't fulfilling for me. Every morning, I'd wake up dreading the day ahead while feeling guilty because I knew I was fortunate. I had stability, a good paycheck, and a career that made sense from the outside. Walking away from that felt almost irresponsible.

Eventually, I realized I needed to stop asking what looked impressive and start asking what actually brought me joy.

Pastry school in Paris changed everything

Baking was my serious hobby for years. If someone had asked me for one bucket-list item, it would have been attending pastry school in France.

So in early 2024, I quit my product management job and moved to Paris. I loved being a student again. After years of working, it felt like such a privilege to ask questions without worrying about performance reviews or promotions.

I started posting videos about pastry school. Those videos unexpectedly took off on social media, and by the time I returned to the US, I had an audience that gave me the confidence to ask, "What if I tried selling pastries?"

I moved to New York, where my partner lived at the time, bought a tiny convection oven and a countertop dough sheeter, and started baking under a cottage food license.

My first preorder sold just 40 pastries.

For the first few months, selling even a dozen boxes felt difficult. But gradually people came back, word of mouth spread, and social media continued to grow. By spring, I realized this could actually become something. By fall, I was consistently selling out pop-ups with lines of customers.

It felt like every small success gave me permission to keep going.

Starting over in San FranciscoMo is testing a July special pastry in her kitchen.

Katherine Li/Business Insider

Then my eight-year relationship ended. Suddenly, it felt like every part of my life was starting over.

Personally, I was rebuilding after the breakup. Professionally, I was leaving behind the customer base I'd spent months building in New York.

I moved back to San Francisco in January and essentially started from scratch. Fortunately, I knew much more than I had the first time around. Within months, I rebuilt my customer base and found a commercial kitchen that could support the specialized equipment I needed.

Now I'm producing around 400 pastries each week and plan to expand to 1,000 with the help of a part-time baking assistant I'm looking to hire.

The trade-offs are real — but so is the joy

Running your own business comes with freedoms I never had in corporate life. I love setting my own schedule and building the kind of workplace culture I want.

But there are trade-offs.

There is no paid time off. If I get sick, there are no pastries to sell and no income. I pay for my own health insurance. I haven't had employer 401(k) contributions, and in my first two years as a business owner, I couldn't contribute to a traditional retirement account because I wasn't paying myself enough.

Starting a small business also means funding your own runway. You're spending money long before you're making much of it.

I think the biggest mindset shift has been believing in myself

When I first started the bakery, I was half in and half out. Part of me assumed I'd probably end up going back to corporate. That hesitation made me pass on opportunities and avoid investments that would have helped the business grow.

Now my mindset is completely different. I believe this business will succeed because I believe in my product and my ability to make it succeed.

I don't think everyone should quit their corporate jobs. Some people genuinely love traditional careers, and that's wonderful.

But if you've done the introspection, you have the financial runway, and you know deep down that your work is making you miserable, don't be afraid to take the next reasonable step.

Life is too short to wake up every morning with a sense of dread. I feel incredibly lucky that now, when I wake up, I feel joy instead.
